The Woman of Tekoa
WUUM-un uv teh-KOH-uh
proper noun
Tekoa, a town of Judah south of Bethlehem, from a Hebrew root meaning “a pitching of tents” or “a trumpet blast.”

Biblical Definition

The woman of Tekoa was a wise woman whom Joab fetched from her town when he perceived that King David’s heart was toward his banished son Absalom. After Absalom had slain his brother Amnon and fled, David mourned but would not recall him. Joab, seeking the king’s relief and his own ends, sent for this woman of discernment and put words in her mouth. Feigning to be a widow in mourning, she came before David with a parable: her two sons had quarrelled in the field, the one slew the other, and now the whole family demanded the survivor’s life, which would quench the last coal left to her and cut off her husband’s name. David, moved, swore to protect her son. Then with great skill she turned his own ruling against him, showing that he had passed sentence on himself while keeping his banished one shut out, and pleaded that God devises means that His banished be not expelled from Him. David discerned Joab’s hand in it, yet granted the substance, and Absalom was brought home. The woman’s wisdom is a study in persuasive, reverent speech that pierces a king’s conscience. Her famous words, that God contrives ways to bring back the outcast, breathe a deeper gospel hope than she perhaps knew, of a God who recalls the banished through a Mediator.

Webster 1828 Definition

A wise woman sent by Joab to King David with a parable, persuading him to recall his banished son Absalom.

expand to see more

THE WOMAN OF TEKOA, a wise woman of Judah employed by Joab.

Joab sent for her to move David’s heart toward the banished Absalom (2Sa 14:2).

She came in mourning attire and told the king a parable of her two sons.

She turned David’s own ruling to plead for the king’s exiled son (2Sa 14:13).

Her words led to Absalom’s recall to Jerusalem.

Key Scripture

2Sa 14:2 — "And Joab sent to Tekoah, and fetched thence a wise woman, and said unto her, I pray thee, feign thyself to be a mourner, and put on now mourning apparel, and anoint not thyself with oil, but be as a woman that had a long time mourned for the dead:"

2Sa 14:13 — "And the woman said, Wherefore then hast thou thought such a thing against the people of God? for the king doth speak this thing as one which is faulty, in that the king doth not fetch home again his banished."

2Sa 14:14 — "For we must needs die, and are as water spilt on the ground, which cannot be gathered up again; neither doth God respect any person: yet doth he devise means, that his banished be not expelled from him."

2Sa 14:20 — "To fetch about this form of speech hath thy servant Joab done this thing: and my lord is wise, according to the wisdom of an angel of God, to know all things that are in the earth."

Modern Corruption

Her parable, especially her word that God devises means that His banished be not expelled, carries a gospel hope of the outcast recalled.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover from the woman of Tekoa is the power of wise, reverent speech to pierce a conscience, and the gospel glimpse in her words. She spoke of a God who devises means that His banished be not expelled from Him, a truth fulfilled in Christ, through whom the outcast sinner is brought home.

Her account also instructs in discernment: David saw Joab’s hand behind her errand yet weighed the substance of her plea. Persuasion need not be deceit when it serves truth, though here it was bent to Joab’s designs. The enduring word is hers: the God of Israel contrives the recall of the banished.

Hebrew Roots

Named for Tekoa, a Judean town meaning “a pitching of tents” or “a trumpet blast.”

expand to see more

The Woman of Tekoa — Tekoa, “a pitching of tents” or “trumpet blast.”

Tekoa lay in the hill country of Judah, south of Bethlehem.

The same town was later home to the prophet Amos.

She is called a “wise woman,” a recognised office of counsel in Israel.

Her speech compared David’s wisdom to that of an angel of God.

Usage

"The woman of Tekoa came before David in mourning to plead a feigned cause."

"By her parable the woman of Tekoa turned the king’s own judgment toward Absalom."

"Few have spoken a deeper gospel word than the woman of Tekoa concerning God’s banished."
